questions.title: What standard of review does the Tenth Circuit apply to BIA asylum decisions and how does it affect factual findings?
questions.question_body: In *Jimenez v. Bondi* the court says it reviews BIA findings of fact under a “substantial‑evidence” standard and may consult the IJ’s explanation. I’m confused about how this standard works in practice: does the appellate court defer to the BIA’s fact‑finding unless there is *no* reasonable evidence, and can it re‑weigh the evidence at all? How does the ability to look at the IJ’s record factor into the analysis?

questions.title: Why are threats alone insufficient to constitute past persecution under the INA?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites *Karki v. Holder* and says “threats alone are insufficient to constitute persecution.” The petitioners suffered repeated death threats and a gunpoint encounter but no physical injury. How have the circuits defined the line between a permissible threat and persecution? Are there any cases where threats were deemed enough, or is physical harm always required?

questions.title: How is the ‘nexus’ requirement satisfied when the persecutor has mixed motives?
questions.question_body: The court discusses the need for a political opinion to be a “central reason” for the harm and notes that mixed‑motive persecution is allowed if the protected ground is at least one central reason. In *Jimenez*, the court concluded the political motive was tangential. What evidentiary tests do courts use to determine whether a protected‑ground motive is "central" rather than peripheral, especially when the persecutor’s actions could be driven by personal or criminal motivations?

questions.title: What constitutes ‘unable or unwilling’ government protection for asylum and withholding claims?
questions.question_body: The opinion emphasizes police reports and the applicant’s efforts to seek protection. How much weight do courts give to a lack of formal reporting versus claims that reporting would be futile or dangerous? Are there precedents where an applicant’s fear of retaliation for reporting satisfied the “unable or unwilling” prong even without an official police complaint?

questions.title: When can an asylum applicant rely on internal relocation as a defense to their claim?
questions.question_body: The court rejected the petitioners’ internal relocation argument, noting they lived safely with relatives for three weeks. What factors do courts consider to decide if an applicant can reasonably relocate within their home country? Does a short‑term safe haven count, and how do courts assess the risk of future persecution after relocation?

questions.title: Why did the Tenth Circuit dismiss the petitioners’ claim for protection under the Convention Against Torture (CAT)?
questions.question_body: The opinion states the petitioners did not appeal the denial of CAT relief, but the BIA’s denial is mentioned. In practice, can a petitioner waive review of a CAT denial by not raising it on appeal, and does the appellate court have any authority to consider it anyway?

questions.title: What is the significance of the “well‑founded fear” presumption from past persecution in asylum cases?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that past persecution gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of a well‑founded future fear. How strong is this presumption in the Tenth Circuit, and what level of evidence is required to overcome it if the applicant’s past persecution claim is weak or borderline?

questions.title: How does the Tenth Circuit treat the discretionary nature of asylum when reviewing BIA decisions?
questions.question_body: The court repeatedly refers to asylum as a discretionary form of relief. Does this discretion mean the appellate court can only look at legal errors and not substitute its own judgment on the merits? How does this discretion interact with the substantial‑evidence standard for factual findings?
